episodes.text: Chose to study physics rather than inherit his family's 300-year-old sake-brewing business, despite his father's explicit, stated expectation from childhood that he would take over the enterprise.

Became so consumed by building his own ham radio equipment as a teenager that he nearly flunked out of school; rather than continue neglecting his studies, he deliberately concentrated on academics for about a year before entering the prestigious Eighth Higher School as a physics major.

Volunteered for the Imperial Japanese Navy rather than wait to be conscripted; while assigned to wartime research on infrared-guided weapons and night-vision gunsights, met electronics engineer Masaru Ibuka, who would become his lifelong business partner.

Learned of Ibuka's postwar radio-repair venture, set up in a bombed-out Tokyo department store, by reading a newspaper article, and actively sought Ibuka out to join him rather than pursue a separate, more conventional postwar career.

Co-founded Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo in May 1946 with about 20 employees, financed by a loan from his own father; the founding prospectus (drafted by Ibuka) explicitly stated the company's purpose as creating a "free-spirited and enjoyable ideal factory" contributing to Japanese culture through technology, rather than a purely profit-oriented charter.

One of the company's earliest products, an electric rice cooker using electrodes to detect when water had steamed away, was clever in concept but routinely under- or over-cooked rice in practice and did not succeed commercially.

When the company's first tape recorder (1950) sold poorly to ordinary consumers, personally demonstrated the machine directly to Japanese schools as a dictation tool rather than abandoning the product, ultimately selling units to nearly one-third of the country's elementary schools.

After a young musician, Norio Ohga, wrote a sharply critical letter comparing the company's poor tape-recorder sound quality to a dancer needing an accurate mirror, brought Ohga in as a paid consultant rather than dismissing the criticism -- Ohga later became Sony's own CEO and chairman.

Committed the still-small company to a large, largely non-recoverable transistor licensing fee from Western Electric (1953) at a time when the wider electronics industry viewed transistors as suited mainly to hearing aids, not the general consumer electronics the company intended to build.

After Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry delayed releasing the foreign currency needed to pay the transistor licensing fee for roughly six months, later drew and stated a general lesson from the episode: "government often impedes innovative change and developments by excessive intervention."

When the new "pocket-sized" transistor radio (1957) proved slightly too large for a standard shirt pocket, instructed sales staff to wear specially tailored shirts with enlarged pockets during demonstrations so the product would visually read as pocket-sized to prospective buyers.

Renamed the company from Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo to the deliberately invented word "Sony" (1958) -- combining the Latin "sonus" with the American nickname "sonny" -- specifically to be pronounceable in any language, years before the company had major international sales to justify a global-facing identity.

Rejected outside offers to market the company's products under existing American brand names, insisting on building Sony's own identity abroad from 1960 onward, and sustained roughly a decade of unprofitable U.S. operations before the American business became a major contributor.

Relocated to the United States with his wife and three children specifically to personally learn the American market before committing further, stating: "you must first learn the market, learn how to sell to it, and build up your corporate confidence before you commit yourself."

Having observed that American professionals routinely moved between employers mid-career, began deliberately hiring experienced mid-career professionals away from competitor firms into Sony on returning to Japan -- against the prevailing Japanese norm of single-company lifetime employment, and in some tension with his own separately-stated "family-like," long-term-loyalty employment philosophy.

At Sony's Rancho Bernardo (San Diego) television plant, deliberately blended Japanese and American management practices -- a non-hierarchical structure, monthly manager-worker meetings, responsive attention to worker welfare -- rather than exporting the Japanese management model unchanged, which led to rejected unionization votes and documented worker loyalty.

Decided that the Betamax videocassette format (1975) would be sold only under the Sony brand, refusing to license it to other manufacturers -- unlike rival VHS, which was licensed broadly -- and later personally acknowledged that this restriction slowed Betamax's ecosystem growth and helped VHS overtake it in the format war.

Pushed forward the Walkman project (1979) against near-unanimous internal opposition -- market research predicted rejection, sales cited an unachievable volume target, marketing called the name embarrassing, and engineers called the four-month deadline impossible -- and personally told Sony's board he would resign if the product failed.

Explicitly stated that he did not believe any amount of market research could have predicted the Walkman's success, framing his own role as anticipating consumer needs people could not yet articulate themselves ("the public does not know what is possible, but we do").

During Walkman development, added a second headphone jack and a volume-lowering "hot line" talk button specifically to address a concern that listening alone via headphones would seem antisocial -- a design compromise that consumers, once the product launched, ignored almost entirely, and that Sony later quietly dropped.

After the Walkman's unconventional park-demonstration launch (June 1979), initial sales were lukewarm -- about 3,000 units in the first month -- a genuine signal the bet might be underperforming, before targeted advertising drove the first 30,000-unit batch to sell out within two months.

Authored a 1966 book ("Never Mind School Records") publicly arguing that Japan's rigid emphasis on academic credentials was not the true determinant of business capability or success -- a position at odds with prevailing Japanese social convention, published while he was himself an elite-university-credentialed businessman.

Co-authored "The Japan That Can Say No" (1989-91) with nationalist politician Shintaro Ishihara, arguing in his own contributed chapters that Japan should abandon postwar deference to the United States and use its economic leverage -- including control over advanced semiconductor supply -- more assertively in bilateral relations.

After unauthorized English translations of "The Japan That Can Say No" caused a significant U.S. controversy, had his own chapters removed from the 1991 authorized English edition, distanced himself from the book's American reception, and stated he had not intended the criticism his chapters were read as making.

Repeatedly and publicly criticized American corporate management's focus on quarterly profits and dividends at the expense of long-term capital investment, and maintained Sony's practice of investing roughly six to ten percent of annual sales into R&D independent of government subsidy or the large industrial-conglomerate structures common in Japan.

An independent biographer's account argues that Sony's costly 1989 Columbia Pictures acquisition (~$4.7 billion) was pursued substantially because senior executives wanted to fulfill Morita's own long-standing personal desire to own a movie studio, rather than from a purely rational strategic case -- a decision the same account frames as costing the company billions.

After a 1993 stroke left him partially paralyzed and largely wheelchair-dependent, continued to exercise real institutional influence rather than being fully sidelined -- notably approving Norio Ohga's selection of Nobuyuki Idei as Sony's next CEO, specifically valuing Idei's marketing background and European business experience.
